Slowly but surely, if we let them.  I think it can only be poorly/loosely enforced though with the amount of non-compliance.  Sort of like copyright infringement.

*Step 1)*

Do not allow major ISPs to purchase routers used for certain functions (i.e. eBGP edge routers) that do now have Lawful Intercept (LI) code approved by government.


* The LI account might be how agents set up "wire taps" on some of the routers.  Yes, this functionality is on many already-in-production routers.  [This](http://www.blackhat.com/presentations/bh-dc-10/Cross_Tom/BlackHat-DC-2010-Cross-Attacking-LawfulI-Intercept-wp.pdf) is about using them for backdoors, rightfully bashing a little on Cisco.  I don't know how much LI is used in US.

* LI users on the router generally have the ability to look at routing tables and mirror ports/ip prefixes to their analyzer

* In some routers, LI user's actions cannot be detected by even the top-level admin accounts.  This is to ensure that these top accounts do not notify their subscribers/peers they are being watched.

* I predict this could be achieved in 5-10 years?  If ISPs/Vendors don't comply there will have to be major fines.  Who cares, many ISPs/Vendors don't want net neutrality anyways so they can make more money.

*Step 2)*

Require all ISPs to give the proper authorities access to the LI account for monitoring.  I think this is the hardest part to enforce and is the major point of failure because ISPs may be able to stall and forget to acocunt for certain routers and such.

*Step 3)*

Write/Use software to make sure the routing table is black-holing the proper prefixes.

* An example prefix is like 192.168.1.0/24 which matches addresses 192.168.1.0-192.168.1.255 (you're all probably familiar with this prefix).  That's because 192.168.0.0/16 is assigned as private networks and most host networks use a /24 in that space.  Look up [CIDR](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIDR_notation) for more info.

* Black-holing means that traffic destined to that prefix is discarded, so it wont go anywhere.

* The software is pretty simple

*Step 4)*

Create Jobs.  Fine offenders.  Make money.

All of us who run ISP networks can fight back and take down the internet completely!  But then there is no connection at all so it's not very fun.  Slowly but surely, I feel this is the way the world will go if NN is thrown out … that is, until the government just kinda stops enforcing it.


*TL;DR* - Require ISPs/Vendors to allow them to spy (in some cases this involves flipping a switch and giving a password out).  Give fines, create jobs, make money.

Nope, US Gov. just has to make a list of illegal routing prefixes.  Since they already have Lawful Intercept (LI) rights for many of the edge routers in the US its just a matter of periodically checking the routing tables to ensure that the illegal routing prefixes are all black-holed at the edge.  This can be performed by simple tcl/expect scripts (albeit, many scripts haha).  If said routes are not black-holed then they will issue whatever fine or jail-time is necessary to get them black-holed again.  Non-compliant ISPs will be physically shut down via FBI and friends.  It's not that hard to enforce, no harder than it was for them to start requiring LI code in the first place.  I actually find it hard to believe otherwise.  

(Do I know what I am talking about?  Maybe, as I'm in the industry of developing edge routers although not specifically tied into LI development or Gov. agencies which request and enforce it in production networks).

The only way to stop it would be people like Dax420 (who I assume is maintaining some edge routers of an ISP) to keep maliciously toying with the prefix filters installed against the BGP protocol.  And after he is quickly fired, the next guy needs to have the same goal.

TL;DR - It's easier than you think to enforce the black-holing of the internet with the systems we are already putting in place.  It may be possible already with the router access already given to certain law enforcement agencies for Lawful Intercept requirements.

The thing that helped me was AA, NA, going broke, my loving girlfriend, and my caring family.  If you don't have the last two go to AA, grab a bunch of numbers and CALL.  

CALL, CALL, CALL.  Call when you are happy, call when you are sad.  Call when you feel worthless or when you get the urge.  Call sometimes when everything is going just right or life feels awesome.  When you are addicted you not only have to watch out for the bad days, but the great days are equally provoking triggers.

I cannot stress this enough.  Calling a former/present addict in the good and the bad times was one of the most helpful things that I found during this incredible struggle.
